title: Knuth's Optimization
html:
Knuth's optimization, also known as the Knuth-Yao Speedup, is a special case of dynamic programming on ranges, that can optimize the time complexity of solutions by a linear factor, from O(n3)O(n^3)O(n3) for standard range DP to O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2).

Conditions

The Speedup is applied for transitions of the form

dp(i,j)=min⁡i≤k<j[dp(i,k)+dp(k+1,j)+C(i,j)].dp(i, j) = \min_{i \leq k < j} [ dp(i, k) + dp(k+1, j) + C(i, j) ].dp(i,j)=i≤k<jmin​[dp(i,k)+dp(k+1,j)+C(i,j)].

Similar to divide and conquer DP, let opt(i,j)opt(i, j)opt(i,j) be the maximum value of kkk that minimizes the expression in the transition (optoptopt is referred to as the "optimal splitting point" further in this article). The optimization requires that the following holds:

opt(i,j−1)≤opt(i,j)≤opt(i+1,j).opt(i, j-1) \leq opt(i, j) \leq opt(i+1, j).opt(i,j−1)≤opt(i,j)≤opt(i+1,j).

We can show that it is true when the cost function CCC satisfies the following conditions for a≤b≤c≤da \leq b \leq c \leq da≤b≤c≤d:

  1. C(b,c)≤C(a,d)C(b, c) \leq C(a, d)C(b,c)≤C(a,d);

  2. C(a,c)+C(b,d)≤C(a,d)+C(b,c)C(a, c) + C(b, d) \leq C(a, d) + C(b, c)C(a,c)+C(b,d)≤C(a,d)+C(b,c) (the quadrangle inequality [QI]).

This result is proved further below.

Algorithm

Let's process the dp states in such a way that we calculate dp(i,j−1)dp(i, j-1)dp(i,j−1) and dp(i+1,j)dp(i+1, j)dp(i+1,j) before dp(i,j)dp(i, j)dp(i,j), and in doing so we also calculate opt(i,j−1)opt(i, j-1)opt(i,j−1) and opt(i+1,j)opt(i+1, j)opt(i+1,j). Then for calculating opt(i,j)opt(i, j)opt(i,j), instead of testing values of kkk from iii to j−1j-1j−1, we only need to test from opt(i,j−1)opt(i, j-1)opt(i,j−1) to opt(i+1,j)opt(i+1, j)opt(i+1,j). To process (i,j)(i,j)(i,j) pairs in this order it is sufficient to use nested for loops in which iii goes from the maximum value to the minimum one and jjj goes from i+1i+1i+1 to the maximum value.

Generic implementation

Though implementation varies, here's a fairly generic example. The structure of the code is almost identical to that of Range DP.


int solve() {
    int N;
    ... // read N and input
    int dp[N][N], opt[N][N];

    auto C = [&](int i, int j) {
        ... // Implement cost function C.
    };

    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        opt[i][i] = i;
        ... // Initialize dp[i][i] according to the problem
    }

    for (int i = N-2; i >= 0; i--) {
        for (int j = i+1; j < N; j++) {
            int mn = INT_MAX;
            int cost = C(i, j);
            for (int k = opt[i][j-1]; k <= min(j-1, opt[i+1][j]); k++) {
                if (mn >= dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + cost) {
                    opt[i][j] = k; 
                    mn = dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + cost; 
                }
            }
            dp[i][j] = mn; 
        }
    }

    return dp[0][N-1];
}

Complexity

A complexity of the algorithm can be estimated as the following sum:

∑i=1N∑j=i+1N[opt(i+1,j)−opt(i,j−1)]=∑i=1N∑j=iN−1[opt(i+1,j+1)−opt(i,j)].\sum\limits_{i=1}^N \sum\limits_{j=i+1}^N [opt(i+1,j)-opt(i,j-1)] = \sum\limits_{i=1}^N \sum\limits_{j=i}^{N-1} [opt(i+1,j+1)-opt(i,j)].i=1∑N​j=i+1∑N​[opt(i+1,j)−opt(i,j−1)]=i=1∑N​j=i∑N−1​[opt(i+1,j+1)−opt(i,j)].

As you see, most of the terms in this expression cancel each other out, except for positive terms with j=N−1j=N-1j=N−1 and negative terms with i=1i=1i=1. Thus, the whole sum can be estimated as

∑k=1N[opt(k,N)−opt(1,k)]=O(n2),\sum\limits_{k=1}^N[opt(k,N)-opt(1,k)] = O(n^2),k=1∑N​[opt(k,N)−opt(1,k)]=O(n2),

rather than O(n3)O(n^3)O(n3) as it would be if we were using a regular range DP.

On practice

The most common application of Knuth's optimization is in Range DP, with the given transition. The only difficulty is in proving that the cost function satisfies the given conditions. The simplest case is when the cost function C(i,j)C(i, j)C(i,j) is simply the sum of the elements of the subarray S[i,i+1,...,j]S[i, i+1, ..., j]S[i,i+1,...,j] for some array (depending on the question). However, they can be more complicated at times.

Note that more than the conditions on the dp transition and the cost function, the key to this optimization is the inequality on the optimum splitting point. In some problems, such as the optimal binary search tree problem (which is, incidentally, the original problem for which this optimization was developed), the transitions and cost functions will be less obvious, however, one can still prove that opt(i,j−1)≤opt(i,j)≤opt(i+1,j)opt(i, j-1) \leq opt(i, j) \leq opt(i+1, j)opt(i,j−1)≤opt(i,j)≤opt(i+1,j), and thus, use this optimization.

Proof of correctness

To prove the correctness of this algorithm in terms of C(i,j)C(i,j)C(i,j) conditions, it suffices to prove that

opt(i,j−1)≤opt(i,j)≤opt(i+1,j)opt(i, j-1) \leq opt(i, j) \leq opt(i+1, j)opt(i,j−1)≤opt(i,j)≤opt(i+1,j)

assuming the given conditions are satisfied.

Lemma

dp(i,j)dp(i, j)dp(i,j) also satisfies the quadrangle inequality, given the conditions of the problem are satisfied.

Proof

The proof for this lemma uses strong induction. It has been taken from the paper Efficient Dynamic Programming Using Quadrangle Inequalities, authored by F. Frances Yao, which introduced the Knuth-Yao Speedup (this particular statement is Lemma 2.1 in the paper). The idea is to induct on the length l=d−al = d - al=d−a. The case where l=1l = 1l=1 is trivial. For l>1l > 1l>1 consider 2 cases:

  1. b=cb = cb=c
    The inequality reduces to dp(a,b)+dp(b,d)≤dp(a,d)dp(a, b) + dp(b, d) \leq dp(a, d)dp(a,b)+dp(b,d)≤dp(a,d) (This assumes that dp(i,i)=0dp(i, i) = 0dp(i,i)=0 for all iii, which is the case for all problems using this optimization). Let opt(a,d)=zopt(a,d) = zopt(a,d)=z.

    • If z<bz < bz<b,
      Note that

      dp(a,b)≤dpz(a,b)=dp(a,z)+dp(z+1,b)+C(a,b).dp(a, b) \leq dp_{z}(a, b) = dp(a, z) + dp(z+1, b) + C(a, b).dp(a,b)≤dpz​(a,b)=dp(a,z)+dp(z+1,b)+C(a,b).

      Therefore,

      dp(a,b)+dp(b,d)≤dp(a,z)+dp(z+1,b)+dp(b,d)+C(a,b)dp(a, b) + dp(b, d) \leq dp(a, z) + dp(z+1, b) + dp(b, d) + C(a, b)dp(a,b)+dp(b,d)≤dp(a,z)+dp(z+1,b)+dp(b,d)+C(a,b)

      From the induction hypothesis, dp(z+1,b)+dp(b,d)≤dp(z+1,d)dp(z+1, b) + dp(b, d) \leq dp(z+1, d)dp(z+1,b)+dp(b,d)≤dp(z+1,d). Also, it is given that C(a,b)≤C(a,d)C(a, b) \leq C(a, d)C(a,b)≤C(a,d). Combining these 2 facts with above inequality yields the desired result.

    • If z≥bz \geq bz≥b, the proof of this case is symmetric to the previous case.

  2. b<cb < cb<c
    Let opt(b,c)=zopt(b, c) = zopt(b,c)=z and opt(a,d)=yopt(a, d) = yopt(a,d)=y.

    • If z≤yz \leq yz≤y,

      dp(a,c)+dp(b,d)≤dpz(a,c)+dpy(b,d)dp(a, c) + dp(b, d) \leq dp_{z}(a, c) + dp_{y}(b, d)dp(a,c)+dp(b,d)≤dpz​(a,c)+dpy​(b,d)

      where

      dpz(a,c)+dpy(b,d)=C(a,c)+C(b,d)+dp(a,z)+dp(z+1,c)+dp(b,y)+dp(y+1,d).dp_{z}(a, c) + dp_{y}(b, d) = C(a, c) + C(b, d) + dp(a, z) + dp(z+1, c) + dp(b, y) + dp(y+1, d).dpz​(a,c)+dpy​(b,d)=C(a,c)+C(b,d)+dp(a,z)+dp(z+1,c)+dp(b,y)+dp(y+1,d).

      Using the QI on CCC and on the dp state for the indices z+1≤y+1≤c≤dz+1 \leq y+1 \leq c \leq dz+1≤y+1≤c≤d (from the induction hypothesis) yields the desired result.

    • If z>yz > yz>y, the proof of this case is symmetric to the previous case.

This completes the proof of the lemma.

Now, consider the following setup. We have 2 indices i≤p≤q<ji \leq p \leq q < ji≤p≤q<j. Set dpk=C(i,j)+dp(i,k)+dp(k+1,j)dp_{k} = C(i, j) + dp(i, k) + dp(k+1, j)dpk​=C(i,j)+dp(i,k)+dp(k+1,j).

Suppose we show that

dpp(i,j−1)≥dpq(i,j−1)  ⟹  dpp(i,j)≥dpq(i,j).dp_{p}(i, j-1) \geq dp_{q}(i, j-1) \implies dp_{p}(i, j) \geq dp_{q}(i, j).dpp​(i,j−1)≥dpq​(i,j−1)⟹dpp​(i,j)≥dpq​(i,j).

Setting q=opt(i,j−1)q = opt(i, j-1)q=opt(i,j−1), by definition, dpp(i,j−1)≥dpq(i,j−1)dp_{p}(i, j-1) \geq dp_{q}(i, j-1)dpp​(i,j−1)≥dpq​(i,j−1). Therefore, applying the inequality to all i≤p≤qi \leq p \leq qi≤p≤q, we can infer that opt(i,j)opt(i, j)opt(i,j) is at least as much as opt(i,j−1)opt(i, j-1)opt(i,j−1), proving the first half of the inequality.

Now, using the QI on some indices p+1≤q+1≤j−1≤jp+1 \leq q+1 \leq j-1 \leq jp+1≤q+1≤j−1≤j, we get

dp(p+1,j−1)+dp(q+1,j)≤dp(q+1,j−1)+dp(p+1,j)  ⟹  (dp(i,p)+dp(p+1,j−1)+C(i,j−1))+(dp(i,q)+dp(q+1,j)+C(i,j))≤(dp(i,q)+dp(q+1,j−1)+C(i,j−1))+(dp(i,p)+dp(p+1,j)+C(i,j))  ⟹  dpp(i,j−1)+dpq(i,j)≤dpp(i,j)+dpq(i,j−1)  ⟹  dpp(i,j−1)−dpq(i,j−1)≤dpp(i,j)−dpq(i,j)\begin{align} &dp(p+1, j-1) + dp(q+1, j) ≤ dp(q+1, j-1) + dp(p+1, j) \\ \implies& (dp(i, p) + dp(p+1, j-1) + C(i, j-1)) + (dp(i, q) + dp(q+1, j) + C(i, j)) \\ \leq& (dp(i, q) + dp(q+1, j-1) + C(i, j-1)) + (dp(i, p) + dp(p+1, j) + C(i, j)) \\ \implies& dp_{p}(i, j-1) + dp_{q}(i, j) ≤ dp_{p}(i, j) + dp_{q}(i, j-1) \\ \implies& dp_{p}(i, j-1) - dp_{q}(i, j-1) ≤ dp_{p}(i, j) - dp_{q}(i, j) \\ \end{align}⟹≤⟹⟹​dp(p+1,j−1)+dp(q+1,j)≤dp(q+1,j−1)+dp(p+1,j)(dp(i,p)+dp(p+1,j−1)+C(i,j−1))+(dp(i,q)+dp(q+1,j)+C(i,j))(dp(i,q)+dp(q+1,j−1)+C(i,j−1))+(dp(i,p)+dp(p+1,j)+C(i,j))dpp​(i,j−1)+dpq​(i,j)≤dpp​(i,j)+dpq​(i,j−1)dpp​(i,j−1)−dpq​(i,j−1)≤dpp​(i,j)−dpq​(i,j)​​

Finally,

dpp(i,j−1)≥dpq(i,j−1)  ⟹  0≤dpp(i,j−1)−dpq(i,j−1)≤dpp(i,j)−dpq(i,j)  ⟹  dpp(i,j)≥dpq(i,j)\begin{align} &dp_{p}(i, j-1) \geq dp_{q}(i, j-1) \\ &\implies 0 \leq dp_{p}(i, j-1) - dp_{q}(i, j-1) \leq dp_{p}(i, j) - dp_{q}(i, j) \\ &\implies dp_{p}(i, j) \geq dp_{q}(i, j) \end{align}​dpp​(i,j−1)≥dpq​(i,j−1)⟹0≤dpp​(i,j−1)−dpq​(i,j−1)≤dpp​(i,j)−dpq​(i,j)⟹dpp​(i,j)≥dpq​(i,j)​​

This proves the first part of the inequality, i.e., opt(i,j−1)≤opt(i,j)opt(i, j-1) \leq opt(i, j)opt(i,j−1)≤opt(i,j). The second part opt(i,j)≤opt(i+1,j)opt(i, j) \leq opt(i+1, j)opt(i,j)≤opt(i+1,j) can be shown with the same idea, starting with the inequality dp(i,p)+dp(i+1,q)≤dp(i+1,p)+dp(i,q)dp(i, p) + dp(i+1, q) ≤ dp(i+1, p) + dp(i, q)dp(i,p)+dp(i+1,q)≤dp(i+1,p)+dp(i,q).

This completes the proof.
